extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and mathematical researchers (graduate and senior researchers interested in foundations and major open problems)
extracted.subtask_description: A broad research agenda listing foundational and specific open problems across mathematics (geometry, analysis, number theory, algebra, topology, mechanics) together with methodological desiderata about axioms, rigor, and analytic versus differentiable hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questioning the necessity of differentiability in Lie's theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate whether the assumption of differentiability of the functions defining continuous groups (as used by Lie) is unavoidable, or whether differentiability can be derived from the group concept together with other geometrical axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek approaches that transform a given group into one whose defining functions are differentiable (possibly by introducing new variables/parameters), or prove differentiability from weaker hypotheses; note that continuity may be retained while differentiability is questioned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain continuity but minimize differentiability postulates
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep continuity as a postulate for geometrical and arithmetical applications, but avoid forcing differentiability into the foundational axioms unless it can be justified or derived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use continuity where it follows naturally from axioms (axiom of continuity); attempt reductions to analytic groups under simple assumptions (e.g., transitivity + existence of certain derivatives as in Schur's theorem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to analytic groups where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that, under suitable hypotheses (e.g., group transitivity and existence of first and some second derivatives), a continuous group can be reduced to an analytic group so that Lie's analytic methods apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference Lie's announced theorem (proved by Schur) as a paradigm; search for variable/parameter transformations that yield analyticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study functional equations without assuming differentiability
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate functional equations (Abel-type, difference equations, others) under hypotheses weaker than differentiability, determining which conclusions still hold or how they must be modified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for existence proofs that derive differentiability from functional/difference equations, and be aware of analytic functional equations that nevertheless admit only nondifferentiable solutions (examples via trigonometric series/Borel–Picard constructions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical axiomatization of physical sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat physical theories (e.g., mechanics, kinetic theory, probability) by axioms in the same rigorous manner as geometry, aiming to include broad classes of phenomena with few axioms and to adjoin axioms to specialize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accompany logical investigation of axioms with rigorous development of relevant mathematical methods (e.g., method of mean values for kinetic theory); mathematicians should test compatibility of new hypotheses rather than rely solely on physical intuition or experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exact formulation and compatibility testing of axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulate axioms precisely and test in each instance whether new axioms are compatible with prior ones; demand proofs of compatibility rather than empirical plausibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The effort to prove compatibility forces exactness in axiom statements; strive for small axiom sets that generate large theory classes and for procedures to check consistency/compatibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate arithmetic properties of transcendental functions' values
rubrics_metrics.description: Study whether special transcendental functions take algebraic or transcendental values at algebraic arguments (e.g., e^{i z} at algebraic irrational z), and develop new methods to determine irrationality/transcendence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate such statements into geometric forms (e.g., trigonometric relations in triangles) and expect novel methods beyond existing ones of Hermite and Lindemann.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate distribution of prime numbers and Riemann's conjecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursue a proof that nontrivial zeros of the zeta function have real part 1/2 and refine Riemann's formula for the prime-counting function, including growth of the error term and the influence of zeros on local prime condensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After Riemann hypothesis progress, further tasks include detailed testing of Riemann's series and exploring consequences (e.g., on error bounds and prime clustering).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attack additive prime problems (Goldbach, twin primes) and prime-linear diophantine equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Work toward proofs of Goldbach's conjecture (every integer as sum of two primes), existence of infinitely many twin primes, and solvability in primes of linear Diophantine equations ax + by + c = 0 under coprimality assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are highlighted as important and difficult next steps once distribution results improve; methods may build on analytic number theory advances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply prime distribution methods to ideal primes in number fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Extend distribution-theory techniques from rational primes to the distribution of ideal primes in number fields, studying associated zeta- or L-functions k(s) defined by sums over ideals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop and analyze the field-specific series and norms (n(j)) to generalize prime-distribution results to number fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove the general law of reciprocity in any number field
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish the reciprocity law for l-th power residues in arbitrary number fields for l odd prime, powers of 2, and powers of odd primes, generalizing reciprocity theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use generalizations of the theory of l-th roots of unity and methods from relative quadratic fields; this arithmetic law is central to broader Kronecker-type extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide solvability of general Diophantine equations by finite procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Devise an effective process that determines, by finitely many operations, whether a given Diophantine equation with integer coefficients is solvable in integers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek algorithms or decision procedures for arbitrary Diophantine equations (Hilbert's Tenth Problem formulation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of quadratic forms with algebraic coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop the theory of quadratic forms with any number of variables and with arbitrary algebraic numerical coefficients, including solving such quadratic equations in integers or fractional numbers within the appropriate algebraic realm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build on existing knowledge of quadratic number fields and study representation problems in general algebraic coefficient settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extend Kronecker's theorem to general algebraic fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalize Kronecker's theorem (abelian number fields arise from roots of unity) to imaginary quadratic fields and ultimately to arbitrary algebraic fields, providing function-theoretic analogues (e.g., elliptic or other functions playing the role of exponentials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use both the arithmetic side (general reciprocity laws, class field theory) and the function-theoretical side (analogies with algebraic function theory, Riemann–Roch analogues) to construct required functions and numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of nomographic construction and representability by functions of two arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether roots of general equations (e.g., seventh degree) can be represented by continuous functions constructed from compositions/inserts of functions of two arguments (nomography), and prove impossibility results when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify classes of multivariable functions not obtainable by finite chains of binary-argument functions; nomography with auxiliary movable elements may extend representability in some cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finiteness of relatively integral functions (finite field of integrality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that for given integral rational functions X1,...,Xm of variables x1,...,xn, the set of rational functions in X1,...,Xm that become integral after substitution constitutes a finite field of integrality—i.e., is generated by finitely many relatively integral functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider refined versions with integer coefficients and divisibility conditions (powers of primes), and attempt to prove finiteness uniformly across exponents; connect to elimination theory and Kronecker's algebraic modular systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous foundation for Schubert's enumerative calculus
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide rigorous proofs and exact limits of validity for enumerative geometric counts that Schubert obtained using the principle of special position (conservation of number).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform explicit eliminations for special-form equations so degrees and multiplicities of solutions are controlled and foreseen; algebra alone 'in principle' is not sufficient—carry out actual elimination processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topology of algebraic curves and surfaces (relative position and sheet counts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate the maximum number and relative positions of closed branches of plane algebraic curves of order n (beyond Harnack's bounds), the number/form/position of sheets of algebraic surfaces, and related questions (e.g., maximum number of Poincaré boundary cycles for differential equations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use continuous variation of coefficients and other topological methods; specific open questions include configurations for sextic curves and sheet counts for quartic surfaces in three-space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression of definite forms by sums/quotients of squares
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether every definite rational integral form (nonnegative for all real variable values) can be expressed as a quotient of sums of squares of forms, possibly with coefficients from the original realm of rationality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note known negative results for representation by sums of squares directly; seek affirmative results for quotients of sums of squares and questions about coefficient fields (answered for ternary forms by Hilbert).

rubrics_metrics.name: Space tiling and dense packing by congruent polyhedra
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify groups of motions with fundamental regions in different constant-curvature spaces and determine whether there exist polyhedra that are not fundamental regions but nevertheless tile space by congruent copies; determine densest packings of equal solids (spheres, tetrahedra) in space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use results on motions in elliptic, Euclidean, and hyperbolic spaces, and exploit group-theoretic finiteness theorems (e.g., Jordan) to guide classification; investigate densest arrangements for applications in number theory, physics, chemistry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize analytic functions as central class for study
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus study on analytic functions as the class most important to science because they include the wealth of functions arising in number theory, differential equations, algebraic functional equations, geometry, and mathematical physics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious of classes that are too narrow (algebraic differential eqs) or too wide (merely smooth functions); analytic functions permit use of power series and strong determination properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyticity of solutions of regular variational problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate whether solutions of regular problems in the calculus of variations (with analytic integrands F satisfying suitable inequalities) are necessarily analytic functions of the independent variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study Lagrangian PDEs of regular variational problems (e.g., potential equation, minimal surface equation) to determine if they admit only analytic integrals; examine boundary-value constraints that are continuous but nonanalytic (Dirichlet problems) and known counterexamples (surfaces with all derivatives but nonanalytic).

rubrics_metrics.name: General existence theory for boundary-value problems of PDEs
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop general principles extending Dirichlet's principle and methods of Schwarz, Neumann, Poincaré to broader boundary-value problems (e.g., prescribed derivatives on boundary, surfaces of least area, constant positive Gaussian curvature surfaces), proving existence of solutions for PDEs with complex boundary prescriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current classical methods handle mainly potential equations; new general principles are needed for variational PDEs and those arising in geometry and physics.
